analysis.one_liner: Lets a state's governor exempt farmers from Clean Air and Clean Water Act rules deemed burdensome.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or a vote: it sat in two House committees and their subcommittees until the term ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would let the chief executive of any state declare that a federal environmental requirement is too burdensome for farmers and simply stop applying it to them. It covers the Clean Water Act and the parts of the Clean Air Act not tied to burning fossil fuels — so rules on farm runoff, livestock waste permits, and pesticide application permits could all be waved off. The only check is a 90-day public comment period before the state makes the decision.
analysis.who_benefits: Farm operators, especially large livestock, dairy, and poultry operations, would gain relief from federal permits and pollution-control requirements: manure and runoff discharge permits, spill-prevention planning, and pesticide application permits could be exempted at a governor's discretion.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Farm operators, especially large livestock operations

how_it_helps.text: The bill allows a state's chief executive to exempt farmers from any requirement of the Clean Water Act, or of the Clean Air Act as applied to non-fossil-fuel emissions, upon determining the requirement is unduly burdensome, after a 90-day public comment period.

The bill's findings target several specific compliance burdens on agriculture, including National Pollutant Discharge Elimination System permits for livestock operations and pesticide applications, and oil spill prevention planning for dairy farms.

analysis.who_pays: People downstream and downwind: neighbors of farms would absorb more agricultural runoff, waste discharges, and air emissions, since the governor's exemption would remove federal standards without any substitute state or federal protection.

drawbacks.text: A single state executive could waive federal water and air protections for an entire category of polluters, and the bill requires no substitute standard — pollution that crosses state lines would simply flow into neighboring states' waters.

The determination rests entirely on a finding that a rule is 'unduly burdensome,' a judgment with no defined standard, so a requirement could be set aside without evidence that public health or water quality would be protected some other way.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Some small farmers face real paperwork costs from federal environmental rules, and the 90-day comment period adds a modest check. But the bill's remedy is sweeping: one official's determination could suspend federal clean water and clean air requirements for all farming in a state, with no replacement protection. The public-health cost of that tradeoff is not mitigated anywhere in the bill.

outcome.mechanism: The House referred it to two committees, which passed it to subcommittees, and it never came back out — no hearing, no markup, no vote — before the term ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Tim Walberg introduced the bill on March 20, 2013, and the House referred it to the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Transportation and Infrastructure Committee.
Within days it was sent to the Water Resources and Environment Subcommittee and the Energy and Power Subcommittee, where it remained without action for the rest of the 113th Congress.
The bill never reached the House floor and no vote was ever taken on it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nothing changed: federal clean water and clean air requirements continued to apply to agriculture, so people who rely on clean rivers, lakes, and air are no worse off. Farm operators seeking exemptions also gained nothing, since the bill died.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: People who rely on clean water

for.name: Rep. Tim Walberg
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and issued findings framing EPA farm rules as overly burdensome.

sides.party_line_note: All 20 sponsors were Republicans; no Democrat supported the bill, and no opposition was ever recorded because it never advanced.

industries.industry: Large livestock, dairy, and poultry operations
industries.note: These operations face the most federal permitting — manure discharge permits, spill prevention plans (including the milk-versus-petroleum dispute the bill's findings cite), and expanding discharge rules — so a governor's exemption would remove their compliance costs while shifting waste and runoff onto surrounding communities and waterways.

The bill would let states exempt pesticide applications from Clean Water Act permits that a federal appeals court required; applicators save permitting costs, while waterways lose the permit system's oversight of pesticide spraying near water.
